summary: For ages 7–8, extend the earlier 'water, light, warmth' idea to the full set of five plant requirements — air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow — with deliberate attention to the two children routinely omit: AIR (plants need it too, not just animals) and ROOM/space (crowded plants compete and grow poorly). The distinctive Year-3 move is COMPARISON: different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements (a cactus thrives on little water; a fern needs lots and shade), so 'requirements vary from plant to plant'. Teach through comparative fair tests (vary one factor, including crowding and nutrients, across plant types) and by matching plants to the conditions they prefer, linking this to habitat/adaptation. Keep 'nutrients from soil' as minerals for health, not the plant's food or source of mass, so the later 'plants make their own food from air and water' idea stays open.
misconceptions: Omitting air and room to grow — listing only water and light as plant needs.
Assuming all plants need identical conditions/amounts (watering a cactus like a fern).
Believing plants 'eat' soil / that soil nutrients are the plant's food and the source of its mass (should be minerals-for-health only at this stage).
Thinking more of any requirement is always better (over-watering, no limit to fertiliser).
Not recognising that overcrowding harms plants (seeing 'more plants together' as fine).
Treating light as optional if the plant is watered (carryover from the Y2 misconception).

activities.title: Plant compare-lab: same care, different outcomes
steps: Use an interactive compare-lab (a simulated side-by-side setup) to grow a cactus and a fern together, with dials for water, light, nutrients and how tightly each is planted, plus an air toggle, so you can adjust conditions and time-lapse growth; pair this with a real cactus and fern on the windowsill to ground the comparison in living plants you tend.
Set each plant's conditions and compare how each responds to the same settings.

Predict before observing, and say why: what will happen to each plant if you turn BOTH plants' water up high? Keep a second cactus and fern on low water to compare against. Then watch what happens — in the compare-lab the high-water fern flourishes while the high-water cactus yellows and rots, unlike the low-water cactus (with real plants, treat this as the expected tendency over a fortnight, not a guaranteed result).
State in your own words why the SAME generous watering helps one plant and harms the other.

Crowd several seedlings of the same kind tightly together and compare them with well-spaced seedlings given the same water and light, watching how the crowded ones compete for space, light, water and nutrients and tend to grow weaker, thinner or smaller (real seedlings may instead grow tall and spindly).
Use the air toggle and consider air as a requirement too: plants need air as well as animals.
activities.insight: Different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements because they are suited to different homes — so 'more is always better' is false, and 'room to grow' and air are real needs alongside water and light.

activities.title: Match each plant to the conditions it likes
steps: Match plants to their preferred conditions (e.g. cactus → dry/bright; fern → damp/shady), explaining each choice.
Name the five requirements — air, light, water, nutrients, and room — naming especially the ones people forget (air and room).
Decide how much water suits THIS plant: pick a suitable amount for a cactus versus a fern, rather than one amount for all plants.
Given a plant with thick, waxy leaves, infer what you would guess about how much water it needs, and say why.
activities.insight: A plant thrives where its needs are met; reading a plant's features helps you predict the conditions it prefers, which shows that requirements vary from plant to plant.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: water both plants generously
steps: Before observing, predict which of a cactus and a fern will thrive and which will struggle when BOTH are watered equally and generously for a fortnight — and say WHY.
Observe over the fortnight and record what actually happens to each plant.
Explain the result: why the same generous watering hurts a cactus but suits a fern.
Answer probe questions: What happens if you plant twenty seeds crammed in one tiny pot — which need runs short? Which of the five things do people most often forget?
activities.insight: The pre-observation reasoning is the key part: a child who understands that needs vary by plant predicts the cactus suffers from over-watering, while a 'more water is better' model wrongly predicts both thrive.

checkQuestion: A cactus from the desert and a leafy fern from the forest floor are grown side by side, and I water BOTH of them a lot every single day. One thrives and one struggles. Which struggles — and the important part, why do two plants not need the same amount of the same things?
checkAnswer: The CACTUS struggles with lots of water — it's adapted to little water and its roots rot if over-watered; the fern is fine with plenty. Different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements (air, light, water, nutrients, space) because they're suited to different homes. Full marks say the cactus suffers from too much water AND generalise that needs vary between plants.
